summary: Describes how to use the ITU-T V.44 compression method for IP Payload Compression, which is defined in RFC 2393. It lets packet contents be compressed before sending. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Zipping a file makes it smaller before you send it. This describes one zipping method for the contents of network packets.

subtitle: Using V.44 compression to make IP packets smaller

tldr.problem: Network packets carrying data can be large, which wastes bandwidth, especially for applications like web pages and email. Compressing the payload before transmission can reduce the amount of data that needs to be sent.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3051 describes how to use the ITU-T V.44 compression algorithm (specifically the LZJH algorithm it is based on) to compress the data portion of IP packets, working with RFC 2393's IP Payload Compression Protocol (IPComp).
tldr.outcome: Packet payloads can be compressed before transmission and decompressed on arrival, reducing bandwidth usage without requiring changes to applications.

facts.label: Minimum packet threshold
facts.value: ~50 bytes (below which compression typically expands data)

today: RFC 3051 is an Informational document that remains the specification for using V.44 compression with IPComp. It has not been obsoleted. The ITU-T V.44 standard is still in use for compression applications, and implementations of this RFC support bandwidth-efficient data transmission in networks where packet compression is beneficial.

sections.title: Introduction to Payload Compression
sections.content:
Network packets often carry data that can be reduced in size through compression, similar to how a ZIP file reduces file size. RFC 2393 defines IPComp (IP Payload Compression Protocol), a method for compressing the payload (data portion) of IP datagrams independently, one packet at a time.

RFC 3051 specifies how to use a particular compression algorithm, based on the ITU-T V.44 Recommendation, with IPComp. V.44 is a standard from the International Telecommunication Union that was developed for modem compression, but the Packet Method variant works well for compressing individual network packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a packet travels over the network, squeeze the data inside it like zipping a file. When it arrives, unsqueeze it back.

sections.title: The LZJH Compression Algorithm
sections.content:
LZJH is an adaptive, general-purpose, lossless data compression algorithm. It combines characteristics of two classic compression techniques: the LZ78 algorithm (fast to reset between packets) and the LZ77 algorithm (achieves good compression ratios). LZJH was chosen by the ITU-T because it offers fast encoding and decoding with good compression ratios, especially for web content (HTML) and email.

The algorithm maintains a dictionary of 1,525 entries (consuming only 16 kilobytes of memory for IP compression) and encodes unmatched characters as ordinals while matched redundant strings become codewords. The dictionary must be reset before compressing each new packet to ensure each packet can be decompressed independently, even if previous packets are lost or arrive out of order.
sections.plainLanguage: The algorithm remembers common patterns in the data, like repeated words, and replaces them with shorter codes. It can learn from each packet without remembering the previous one.

sections.title: Compression and Decompression Process
sections.content:
The Encoder compresses each datagram payload. It resets its dictionary before processing each packet to ensure independent compression. After the last byte of data is processed, it flushes any remaining output to produce a complete compressed packet. If compression would make the data larger (expand it), the packet is left uncompressed and the IPComp header is omitted.

The Decoder reverses the process. It resets its dictionary before processing each compressed datagram, ensuring independent decompression. If a packet is not compressed, the decoder simply passes the payload data unmodified to the next layer. Padding bytes may appear after the FLUSH codeword; these are ignored by the decoder.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender squeezes each packet before sending, using a fresh dictionary each time. The receiver un-squeezes it with its own fresh dictionary. Both start clean for every packet.

sections.title: Implementation Parameters
sections.content:
The IPComp Association (IPCA) parameters for LZJH compression are minimal. The Transform ID is IPCOMP_LZJH, which can be negotiated using IKE (Internet Key Exchange) or configured manually. No additional security attributes are required for negotiation.

Small packets (around 50 bytes or less) typically do not compress well with LZJH and may actually expand. Implementations may choose not to compress payloads below a threshold size, such as 50 bytes. The V.44 specification also describes an adaptive compressibility test that implementations can optionally use to detect when a particular datagram will not compress well and avoid the overhead of attempting compression.
sections.plainLanguage: Before trying to squeeze a tiny packet, it might be worth checking if squeezing will actually help. Big packets usually compress well, tiny ones usually do not.

sections.title: Practical Considerations and Security
sections.content:
RFC 3051 does not introduce security issues beyond those in RFC 2393. The compression process itself is transparent to security protocols operating above or below IP.

Internet testing shows that LZJH compresses typical web pages and email files effectively, with payloads of approximately 50 bytes or smaller being more likely to expand than compress. The encoder is extremely efficient, capable of encoding a two-character string in just 3 bits after the second occurrence of that string. This makes LZJH suitable for environments where packet loss and out-of-order delivery are possible, such as satellite and wireless networks where IPComp was originally developed.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a straightforward compression technique with no security tricks. It works best on large packets with repeating data, like web pages.
